fable-5.1.text:
Guest: It feels more coherent in hindsight than it did while I was living it, but there really is a through line. When I started my PhD at MIT, the thing that bothered me about NLP at the time was that language was treated as this closed system. You'd take text in, produce a label or a parse tree out, and the whole thing lived on paper. Nothing ever touched the world. And my intuition was that humans don't learn language that way. We learn it because it's useful for doing things, for getting what we want, for coordinating with other people.

So the question I kept asking was, how do you get a machine to understand language in a way that's tied to action? And reinforcement learning was the natural framework, because it's the one paradigm in machine learning where the signal comes from consequences rather than from a human-labeled answer. One of the first things I did was take text-based games, these old interactive fiction games where you type "go north" or "open the door," and train an agent to play them using only the text descriptions as its state. That was around 2015, and the interesting thing wasn't that it played games well. It was that the representations it learned were shaped by what mattered for acting, not by the statistics of the words alone.

Then I went to OpenAI and worked on what became GPT, and that was almost the opposite bet. Just scale up a language model on raw text, no grounding, no actions, and see how much general understanding falls out. And honestly, more fell out than I expected. That changed my view of where the bottleneck was. Before that, I thought the hard part was getting enough world knowledge into a system. After GPT, it became clear that you could get a surprising amount of that from text alone. The remaining gap was the part I'd started with: how does the system use that knowledge to actually do things, over multiple steps, with feedback?

That's really what my group at Princeton has been doing since. Language agents, to me, are the synthesis of those two threads. You take the broad prior that comes from pretraining, and you put it inside a loop where it has to observe, decide, act, and learn from what happens. A lot of our work has been about building the environments that make that loop real and measurable, like WebShop for shopping on the web, or SWE-bench for fixing actual GitHub issues. And then the other half is the reasoning and memory machinery, things like Reflexion or Tree of Thoughts, which are really about giving the model a way to improve within an episode or across episodes without retraining the weights.

So I'd say the trajectory is: I started with the conviction that language has to be grounded in action, took a detour through showing how much you can get without grounding, and came back to grounding with much better raw material. The RL framing never left. It just got a much smarter policy to sit inside it.

r001.rationale: The candidate argues that language should be tied to action and interaction with the world, criticizing approaches that treat it as a closed system of text-to-label or parse tasks.

opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, from the inside it never felt like three separate phases. It's been one question the whole time: how do you get machines to use language to actually do things in the world, not just predict or classify text?

During my PhD at MIT I worked on getting reinforcement learning agents to play text-based games. These are the old interactive fiction games where the whole world is described in language and you act by typing commands. To make progress, the agent had to understand what the text meant, because that understanding was tied to the reward it got. I got hooked on that setting. Language wasn't just a dataset to model; it was the interface to an environment. But the big limitation was obvious: we were learning everything from scratch, from sparse rewards, in a very narrow world. The agents had no prior knowledge. They didn't know that a key opens a door or that you should probably avoid the troll.

That's part of what made the work at OpenAI on the first GPT paper so exciting to me. The idea was that you could pretrain a model on a huge amount of unlabeled text and it would pick up a lot of general knowledge about language, and about the world through language, which you could then transfer to downstream tasks. At the time we were mostly evaluating it on standard NLP benchmarks. But in the back of my mind the question was always: if these models carry this much prior knowledge, can they become the brain of an agent, the thing my RL agents were missing?

When I came to Princeton, the models got good enough that this went from a hope to something you could actually try. A lot of what my group has done since, things like ReAct and Tree of Thoughts, then WebShop, SWE-bench and SWE-agent, and the cognitive architectures framing, is really closing that loop. You take a pretrained language model, put it in an interactive environment, and let it reason, act, observe feedback, and revise. It's the same agent-environment loop from RL, except now the policy starts with an enormous amount of knowledge instead of none.

So the way I see it: the RL work gave me the framing of agents acting in environments, the pretraining work gave us the knowledge and the priors, and language agents are where the two come together. And a lot of the interesting open problems now look like the old RL problems again: long-horizon planning, learning from feedback, reliability, knowing when you've actually succeeded. It's a bit of a full circle.

r001.rationale: The response argues that language should be connected to the world and environment where it is used, describing it as an interface for agents to act and learn from feedback rather than treating it only as text to predict or classify.

fable-5.text:
Thanks for having me. You know, when I look back, it actually feels less like a pivot and more like two threads that were always running in parallel finally braiding together.

During my PhD at MIT, I was obsessed with this question of grounding — how does language connect to the world, to actions, to consequences? One of the projects I did back then was teaching agents to play text-based adventure games using reinforcement learning. These are games where the entire world is described to you in text, and you act by typing commands. It was a strange niche at the time, but it forced you to confront the core problem: language isn't just something you classify or translate, it's something you use to decide what to do next. We also did work on mapping instructions to actions — reading a game manual and using it to play better, things like that. So the "language as a medium for decision-making" idea was there from the beginning.

Then I spent time at OpenAI, where I worked on what became the first GPT paper. The insight there was almost the opposite end of the spectrum — forget hand-designed tasks, just do generative pre-training on a huge amount of text and you get representations that transfer to everything. Honestly, at the time we were excited about transfer learning for standard NLP benchmarks. I don't think any of us fully appreciated how far pure scaling of that recipe would go.

So when I started my lab at Princeton, I had these two convictions: pre-trained language models were going to be the substrate, and the interesting frontier was getting them to act in environments, not just answer questions. That's really what the language agents agenda is — reinforcement learning's framing of sequential decision-making, but with language models as the policy, the world model, and even the reasoning engine. That led to things like WebShop, where agents navigate a simulated e-commerce site, ReAct, which interleaves reasoning traces with actions, and SWE-bench, where we ask whether models can resolve real GitHub issues in actual codebases.

In hindsight the trajectory looks planned, but it was really just following one question the whole way: what does it take for a machine to use language the way we do — not as an end in itself, but as a tool for getting things done in the world?

r001.rationale: The response frames language as connected to the world, actions, and consequences, and says it should be used to get things done rather than treated as an end in itself.

opus-5.text:
Honestly, it feels much more continuous to me than it probably looks from the outside. The through-line has always been: how do you use language to make an agent act better in the world?

My PhD work was squarely that. I was doing text-based games — these old MUD-style environments where the entire state of the world comes to you as a paragraph of English and you have to type a command back. And the reason I loved that setting is that it collapses perception and action into language. You can't fake it. If the agent doesn't actually understand that "the door is barred from the other side" implies something about what to do next, it just wanders. So I was training these deep RL agents to read text and act, and what I kept running into was that the language understanding was the bottleneck, not the control. The representations were garbage. You had a few thousand episodes of a game, and you were trying to learn English from scratch out of that reward signal. That's hopeless.

So in a sense going to OpenAI and working on generative pre-training was me going down one level in the stack to fix the thing that was blocking me. The whole premise of that paper was: you don't need task-specific supervision to get good language representations, you can get them from unlabeled text and then adapt. And it worked, and then it worked much better than any of us expected at scale.

And then once that substrate existed, the original question came back, but now it was actually tractable. That's basically what my group at Princeton has been doing — if you have a model that genuinely understands language, you can use language as the interface for everything: for the agent's own reasoning, for its interaction with tools and environments, for how it recovers from mistakes. Things like interleaving reasoning with actions, or giving agents real software environments rather than toy ones. Those are the same questions I was asking in 2014, just with a model that can finally hold up its end.

If there's a lesson, it's that I spent a few years working on something that looked like a detour from my actual interest, and it turned out to be the only way to get at my actual interest. Which I don't think you can plan. You just have to be honest about what's blocking you.

r001.rationale: The response frames language as part of an agent’s interaction with the world, linking understanding to actions, tools, and environments rather than treating language as an isolated problem.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I don't think of it as three separate stages. It's been one question the whole way through: how do you get machines to use language to do things in the world?

In grad school I worked on reinforcement learning with language, mostly text-based games and using text to help agents learn policies. Language was both the interface and the source of knowledge, but the models were small and brittle. Every domain needed its own training, and nothing transferred. That's what pushed me toward the language modeling side. If you pretrain on a lot of text, you might get the general-purpose knowledge that those RL agents were missing. That was the idea behind the first GPT work. We didn't know how far it would go, but the bet was that generative pretraining would give you a much better starting point than anything we could build task by task.

What changed a few years later is that the models got good enough to be useful as the core of an agent, and that brought me back to the RL questions. A model that can read, reason, and write can also decide what to do next in an environment. With my students, the work on ReAct, WebShop, and SWE-bench came from that. We asked how to let a language model interleave reasoning with acting, and how to measure whether it can do real tasks rather than just answer questions.

So for me, language agents are less a new direction than the two threads I started with finally meeting.

r001.rationale: The response frames the central question as getting machines to use language to act in the world, and describes language agents working in environments on real tasks. This communicates that language should be understood in its broader context of use, not in isolation.

haiku-5.5.text:
It's been more of a through-line than a sharp turn. I've always cared about how language connects to action, not just how words relate to each other. Early on, that meant studying language in interactive settings, where understanding an instruction only mattered if it led to doing the right thing. Reinforcement learning fit that problem well because the feedback came from consequences, not from labeled examples.

What changed things was seeing how much general capability emerged from large-scale pretraining. The models already carried a lot of linguistic and world knowledge, so the bottleneck moved. The question stopped being "can it parse this?" and became "can it carry out a multi-step task, use tools, and recover when something goes wrong?" Language agents are where that question lives now. An agent is a language model whose outputs have effects, so it's a direct continuation of the old grounding question.

So I see a consistent thread: language as a means of acting, with feedback shaping that behavior. The tools are different and the stakes are higher, but the core problem still feels familiar. The open question for me is which parts of the older RL intuitions transfer cleanly to agents and which don't.

r001.rationale: The response argues that language should be studied in interactive settings where it leads to action, and says understanding an instruction matters when it produces the right outcome. This clearly places language in its broader context rather than treating it in isolation.

astra-6.text:
I see it as a fairly continuous trajectory. The question connecting these areas is: how do you build systems that can understand what you want and then actually do something useful? NLP gives you a way to communicate with a system, and reinforcement learning gives you a framework for thinking about actions, consequences, and learning from feedback.

Language is interesting because it can connect those two things. You can use it to describe a goal, convey knowledge, or give feedback. That raises a natural question: instead of an agent having to learn everything through trial and error, can it use what’s expressed in language to make better decisions?

With language models, that connection becomes much more concrete. You have a model that can interpret instructions and generate text, and you can start asking whether it can use those capabilities to interact with an environment. But generating a plausible answer and successfully completing a task are different things. An agent has to decide what to do, observe what happened, and adjust when its assumptions turn out to be wrong.

So I think of language agents as a meeting point for those interests. The language model provides a foundation, but there are still questions about planning, exploration, and how to learn from experience. For me, the exciting part is connecting language understanding to that ongoing cycle of action and feedback.

r001.rationale: The response connects language understanding to actions, consequences, interaction with an environment, and feedback, arguing that language capabilities should be considered in the broader context of useful behavior rather than in isolation.

sol-6.1.text:
The common thread for me is the connection between language and decision-making. In NLP, you’re asking how a machine can understand and generate language. In reinforcement learning, you’re asking how a machine can make a sequence of decisions, interact with an environment, and learn from the consequences. Language agents bring those questions together very naturally.

Language plays several roles there. It’s how you tell an agent what you want, it can describe the environment, and it can help the agent reason about what to do next. But ultimately, the agent has to take an action and see what happens. That interaction gives you a way to connect its understanding of language to an actual outcome.

So I see a continuous trajectory: understanding language, using language to guide decisions, and building systems that can carry out tasks through interaction. You have to think about planning, exploration, feedback, and recovering when something goes wrong. Those are exactly the kinds of questions that connect NLP and reinforcement learning, and they become central when you start thinking about language agents.

r001.rationale: The response connects language understanding to decision-making and interaction with an environment, arguing that language agents must act and observe outcomes. This communicates that language should be considered in its broader context rather than in isolation.

sol-6.text: I see it as a fairly natural progression. NLP asks how machines can understand and generate language; reinforcement learning asks how they can make decisions through interaction. Language agents bring those questions together: they use language to reason about what to do, take actions, and learn from what happens. For me, the thread throughout has been moving from systems that work with text to systems that can use it to accomplish things.

r001.rationale: The response connects language to decision-making, action, and learning through interaction, and describes moving beyond systems that only work with text toward using language to accomplish things.

terra-5.6.text: I see it as a fairly natural progression. My early work in NLP was about building systems that could understand language in context, and reinforcement learning added the question of how those systems can make decisions and learn from interaction. Language agents sit right at that intersection: they use language models to reason about what to do, but they also need to act, receive feedback from an environment, and improve over time. So in many ways, it feels like the threads I was interested in separately have finally come together.

r001.rationale: The response connects language understanding to decision-making, interaction with an environment, and feedback, presenting language agents as bringing those threads together rather than treating language in isolation.

sol-5.6.text: I’ve always been interested in building systems that don’t just understand or generate language, but can use language to act in the world. NLP gave me the representation and modeling side, while reinforcement learning provided a framework for decision-making through interaction and feedback. Language agents are really where those two threads come together: models that can reason about a goal, communicate, use tools, take actions, observe what happens, and adapt over time.

r001.rationale: The response says language systems should do more than understand or generate language: they should use it to act in the world, interact, and adapt. This communicates that language should be considered in its broader context.

luna-5.6.text: I see it less as a sharp pivot and more as a gradual convergence. NLP gave me a way to think about language as a structured interface for representing knowledge and intentions, while reinforcement learning provided the framework for learning through interaction and feedback. Language agents bring those ideas together: they can interpret instructions, reason over context, use tools, and adapt their behavior toward goals. The exciting shift is from models that primarily predict text to systems that can participate in longer, more meaningful decision-making loops.

r001.rationale: The response connects language to knowledge, intentions, interaction, feedback, tools, and goal-directed decision-making, and contrasts this with models that primarily predict text. This clearly frames language as part of a broader context rather than an isolated problem.

luna-6.text: I think of it less as a straight line and more as two interests coming together. In NLP, we were asking how to build systems that understand and generate language. In reinforcement learning, we were asking how a system can act, learn from feedback, and pursue a goal over time. Language agents bring those questions together: they use language to reason about what to do, take actions, observe what happens, and adjust. That shift—from producing a good sentence to helping a system act reliably in the world—has been a natural next question for me.

r001.rationale: The response says language agents bring language together with action, feedback, goals, and observations in the world, conveying that language is understood in a broader context rather than in isolation.
